titulo.texto: Ceremonial Attire of the Mazahua Woman

frase_gancho.texto: Red wool, silver, and deer: the festive dress of the Mazahua woman.

puente_narrativo.texto: From clothing, we move on to the plant that does almost everything. Look for a collection of ropes, bags, and blankets made of golden fiber, crafted from the leaves of the maguey.

guion_corto.texto: This festive dress belongs to Mazahua women, a people of western State of Mexico and eastern Michoacán. The main piece is the chincuete, a long, heavy wool skirt, red or blue, pleated at the waist. It is held in place by a wide, hand-woven sash with designs of deer, birds, and plants. The blouse is made of shiny fabric, with ruffles and embroidery, and is sometimes covered with a shawl or a quechquémitl. The most striking feature is the arracadas, large silver half-moon earrings that jingle as she walks. It is clothing worn at festivals, and it says, with colors and silver, where its wearer comes from.

guion_largo.texto:
When a Mazahua woman dresses in her finest, she is heard before she is seen. Her silver earrings jingle as she walks, and her wool skirt moves with a weight you can notice. The museum shows it standing still, but the dress was made for movement: for walking to church, for dancing at a festival, for crossing a plaza.

The Mazahua live in western State of Mexico and in eastern Michoacán. Their name, which comes from Nahuatl, is usually explained as «people of the deer». And the deer appears right where you would expect it: on the sashes, alongside birds and plants. It is one more deer to add to those you have seen in the [Wixárika (Huichol) Nierika](mna_s13_nierika_estambre) and on the [desert slab](mna_s11_petroglifo_desierto). For many peoples of the country, the deer was a sacred animal, and to this day it leaves its mark on clothing.

Start from the bottom. The chincuete is a long skirt of thick wool, red or blue, which is wrapped around the body and pleated at the waist. It is a heavy garment, made for the cold of the mountains. The wool arrived with the Spaniards’ sheep, so it is an example of how the old and the new were blended: a skirt shape of Indigenous origin, made with a material that came from Europe.

The sash is the most elaborate part. It is long and wide, and it is woven by hand with designs of deer, birds, and plants. It serves to hold the skirt in place, and also to say something: the design is often recognizable, and whoever knows it can tell which community the woman is from. It is a kind of signature woven around the waist.

Then come the jewels. The silver arracadas, shaped like a half-moon, are the most spectacular part. Some carry figures of doves and small bells. The half-moon is a shape you may already know from other places: it appears in Mesoamerican mythology, linked to the Moon. We do not know whether these earrings have that connection, but it is a coincidence that invites reflection.

The festive dress is not an everyday outfit. For work, simpler clothing is worn, and many Mazahua women today wear modern clothes. Some families moved to cities such as Toluca or Mexico City, and there they keep up their festivals and their language, Mazahua. There are those who keep the dress for special occasions, the way one keeps a treasure.

Here is a curiosity that touches anyone who lives in Mexico City: part of the water drunk there comes from the Cutzamala system, whose dams lie on lands where Mazahua communities live. Some Mazahua women have raised their voices to demand clean water for their own towns. Festive dress and the defense of water are two ways of saying the same thing: we are here.

What you see here is a way of saying «I am from here». In a country with so many peoples, clothing works as a silent language. If you learn to read it, you discover that a skirt, a sash, and a pair of earrings can tell where you come from, which festival you are going to, and to whom you belong.

texto: Look for the deer and birds embroidered on the sash
Observe the pleats of the wool skirt at the waist
Look at the silver half-moon earrings

texto.Region: Highlands of the State of Mexico (San Felipe del Progreso, Ixtlahuaca) and Michoacán
texto.Technique/Material: Percale/velvet fabric, wool sash woven on a backstrap loom, hand embroidery and silver metalwork
texto.Function: Ceremonial formal attire, community rank and protection of identity

texto.pregunta: Myth: Indigenous dress is worn only for tourists.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is festive attire for each community’s celebrations. Many women keep it for special occasions, and its designs say where they are from.
